doc.title: Phoebe Jacobs and Jackie Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Racism, class and Katrina's threat to New Orleans culture
summary: Harris discusses racism and competition in New Orleans, Katrina's effect, and how second lines, brass bands and Mardi Gras need the displaced community to return.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: It’s such a rich but sometimes confusing history racially with the Creole influence and all the nationalities there. Has that atmosphere, has a racial atmosphere let’s say pre-Katrina at least, what was it like?

Well you know it’s obvious that there is racism in New Orleans but I mean it still exists. We can’t say that racism existed in New Orleans and say that it was in the past because it’s in the present now. But the unique thing about New Orleans, even in its racism, people in that town, black people and white people live right next door to each other. We eat at the same restaurants. We work in the same locations. But where the racism exists is part of classism and also in the competitive — it’s very competitive there. And where it’s obvious that this competition that has existed has really affected the abilities for people of color to earn a fair wage in that town. I mean Katrina showed us what that was. But I also have to say that in many cases I think that people have the wrong impression of people who have been affected by Katrina because Katrina had showed no racism. There are as many white people who are displaced and who are homeless as black people. If you go out to the Lakefront and to New Orleans East where a lot of affluent African-Americans and white people are, I mean they are, all of those homes are destroyed. And the unfortunate thing is there is no quick movement to really get that part of town rebuilt. I know that the city and the mayor is working, but those of us who are trying to get back home it seems that things are moving at a very snail pace. And let me say that if the people who are living in other states, the black people, are not helped to get back home the culture in New Orleans as we know it will not — it won’t exist anymore. You see when you look at the second line in the brass band parade and social aid and pleasure clubs, that is a legacy that’s in the heritage that was created by African-Americans and it’s being perpetuated by African-Americans. We can bring musicians back home, which we need to bring them all home. But if there are no people in the streets to attend those second lines, then so who are the musicians going to play to, themselves? There’s not © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

enough tourists to really participate in the second lines and tourists don’t really know how to receive those people. So you know people talk about the new New Orleans, what is it going to be? If we as a group of native New Orleaneans and people who were born there and understand the quirks in our culture and teach our children and continue to do those things that make us what we call naturally New Orleans we are going to end up with something that’s really not going to be authentic anymore.
So you need a population — the music is not, it can’t exist in a vacuum.
You need, as you said, people to be in the second line so that those things can happen.

See another thing too is, which is good, New Orleans musicians for the most part play all genres of music. Your traditional jazz artists play rhythm & blues, contemporary and avante garde artists play rhythm and blues, some play Gospel in the churches, some play classical music. And what’s happened now is these bands are separated, they’re divided. Now they’re being called out to meet each other in different cities. But that is not going to last because these people don’t get to practice together anymore, they’re not eating the same red beans and rice and gumbo anymore, they’re not attending the second lines together anymore. I mean there’s a real disconnect there, and you know that connection is what has perpetuated that culture and that atmosphere and that spirit that makes New Orleans what it is. Take Mardi Gras. Mardi Gras is not going to be what it’s been before. I mean we have black Mardi Gras clubs, there are white Mardi Gras clubs, black musicians perform at the balls at these clubs, they perform at the clubs that are hosted by black, you know by the African-American community. All that’s going to be lost.
Wow. It’s a thick and deep subject for sure.
